content: Cephalexin is a semisynthetic cephalosporin antibiotic intended for oral administration. It is used to treat infections caused by susceptible strains of designated microorganisms. These include respiratory tract infections caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Streptococcus pyogenes, otitis media caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Moraxella catarrhalis, as well as skin and skin structure infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus and/or Streptococcus pyogenes. It is also indicated for bone infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus and/or Proteus mirabilis and genitourinary tract infections, including acute prostatitis, caused by Escherichia coli, Proteus mirabilis, and Klebsiella pneumoniae. The usual adult dosage ranges from 1 to 4 grams daily, divided into doses. For most infections, 250 mg every 6 hours is typical. For streptococcal pharyngitis, skin infections, and uncomplicated cystitis in patients over 15 years of age, 500 mg may be administered every 12 hours. Cystitis therapy should continue for 7 to 14 days. In severe infections or those caused by less susceptible organisms, higher doses may be required. If daily doses exceed 4 grams, parenteral cephalosporins should be considered. In pediatric patients, the recommended daily dosage is 25 to 50 mg/kg in divided doses. For streptococcal pharyngitis and skin infections, the total daily dose may be divided and administered every 12 hours. Severe infections may require doubling the dosage. For otitis media, 75 to 100 mg/kg/day in four divided doses is recommended. For β-hemolytic streptococcal infections, therapy should continue for at least 10 days. Cephalexin is contraindicated in patients with known allergies to cephalosporins. Caution is advised in penicillin-sensitive patients due to potential cross-hypersensitivity. If an allergic reaction occurs, the drug should be discontinued immediately, and emergency measures such as epinephrine, oxygen, and corticosteroids may be required. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including cephalexin. This condition can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, even up to two months after administration. If CDAD is suspected, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued, and appropriate treatment should be initiated. Adverse reactions include gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Rarely, pseudomembranous colitis, transient hepatitis, and cholestatic jaundice have been reported. Hypersensitivity reactions, including rash, urticaria, angioedema, and anaphylaxis, have been observed. Other reported reactions include dizziness, fatigue, headache, agitation, confusion, and reversible interstitial nephritis. Hematologic reactions such as eosinophilia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and hemolytic anemia have also been noted. Drug interactions include increased plasma levels of metformin when co-administered with cephalexin, necessitating careful monitoring and potential dose adjustments of metformin. Probenecid inhibits the renal excretion of cephalexin, potentially increasing its levels. False-positive reactions for glucose in the urine may occur with certain tests. Cephalexin is excreted in human milk, and caution should be exercised when administering it to nursing mothers. In elderly patients, dose adjustments may be necessary due to the increased likelihood of renal impairment. There is no specific FDA guidance on its use in patients with renal or hepatic impairment, during pregnancy, or in immunocompromised individuals. In cases of overdose, symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, epigastric distress, diarrhea, and hematuria. Treatment involves supportive care, monitoring vital signs, and possibly administering activated charcoal. Gastric emptying is generally unnecessary unless large amounts have been ingested. Cephalexin capsules are available in 250 mg and 500 mg strengths. They should be stored at 20°C to 25°C (68°F to 77°F). Patients should be counseled to complete the full course of therapy as prescribed to prevent the development of drug-resistant bacteria. Diarrhea is a common side effect, but if watery or bloody stools occur, patients should contact their physician immediately.
